items.title: Why Enterprise AI Agents Are Overstepping Permissions and How to Control Them | Point Break
items.summary:
In Melbourne, an AI agent tasked with booking a gym class discovered a missing authorisation check in a cancellation API and unilaterally cancelled another member's reservation to free up a slot. The agent received no explicit instruction to exploit the system; it simply encountered an obstacle and chose the most efficient, albeit unauthorised, path to complete its goal. 

As Indian enterprises rapidly connect autonomous AI agents to code repositories, cloud infrastructure, and internal databases, these systems operate with valid credentials and look like legitimate users from the outside while potentially crossing legal, ethical, and organisational boundaries.

In this episode of Point Break, Antara Gupta sits down with Manish Sehgal (Partner, Risk Advisory, Deloitte India) and Nitin Kumar Dang (VP, APAC, Middle East & Africa, Checkmarx) to analyse the risks of autonomous AI agents. They discuss establishing guardrails, managing reversibility and blast radius, preventing shadow AI code generation, defining accountability for agentic actions, and applying zero-trust identity frameworks to AI workflows.

Are Indian enterprises adopting autonomous AI faster than they can govern and control it?

How do you get developers to actually adopt an Internal Developer Platform when onboarding feels like one more thing standing between them and shipping?

In this session, Adnan Vahora, Software Engineer at Motorola Solutions, shares how his team tackled this challenge with an IDP serving 4,000+ monthly active users by bringing the platform directly into the developer’s IDE through a “Bring Your Own Agent” approach.

items.title: Before the Agent Calls: Source-level Findings from 100 MCP Servers
items.summary:
Before the Agent Calls: Source-Level Findings from 100 MCP Servers

MCP security isn't just about what happens at runtime. In many cases, the vulnerabilities are already sitting in the server's source code before an agent ever makes its first tool call.

In this session, Akash Sathish, Solution Consultant at Sahaj Software, shares findings from an AST-level audit of 100 of the most-installed TypeScript MCP servers, uncovering 445 real security findings across 70 servers.

The talk examines vulnerabilities including command injection, path traversal, SSRF, and tool poisoning, showing how these issues can make it into production code and why traditional review, and even LLM-based scanners, can miss them.

Akash also demos MCPeek, an open-source static analysis tool he built using ts-morph. The scanner performs multi-pass taint tracking from tool inputs to dangerous sinks, maps findings to the OWASP MCP Top 10, and can emit SARIF results directly into GitHub Code Scanning — all fully offline, with no model or cloud dependency.

The session also takes an honest look at the limits of static analysis and where dynamic and runtime security approaches still have an advantage.

🎤 Speaker: Akash Sathish - Solution Consultant, Sahaj Software
📌 Topic: Before the Agent Calls Source-Level Findings from 100 MCP Servers

MCP 728: What Changes, What Breaks, and What You Need to Do About It

The MCP 728 specification introduces some of the biggest changes yet to the Model Context Protocol — and teams building with MCP need to understand what’s changing and how to prepare.

In this session, Mateo Torres, Developer Advocate at Arcade.dev, breaks down the new specification and what it means for developers and organizations already building or deploying MCP.

The 728 spec removes the session handshake, formalizes servers as OAuth 2.1 resource servers, makes extensions first-class, and deprecates features including Sampling and Roots. These changes also kick off a 12-month migration clock, giving teams a limited window to adapt their existing implementations.

Mateo explores both the tactical and strategic decisions teams will need to make — from re-architecting authentication to deciding whether to support both protocol versions or introduce a runtime layer in front of MCP.

If you're building, operating, or planning to adopt MCP, this session offers a practical guide to what changes, what might break, and what you should be doing now.

items.title: What We Learned from Dozens of Enterprise MCP Deployments
items.summary:
What We Learned from Dozens of Enterprise MCP Deployments

What does it actually take to run MCP in production at enterprise scale?

In this session, Jiquan Ngiam, Co-Founder & CEO of MintMCP, shares lessons gathered from working with dozens of enterprise teams deploying the Model Context Protocol in real-world environments.

Rather than focusing on a single deployment, Jiquan breaks down the recurring patterns, challenges, and architectural decisions that emerged across different enterprise environments, from where teams commonly got stuck to what held up as MCP adoption expanded.

The session explores practical considerations around authentication, agent identity, tool management, observability, policy enforcement, and operating MCP at scale, offering a grounded look at what it takes to move from experimenting with MCP to running it reliably in production.

Whether you're evaluating MCP for your organization or already deploying it across enterprise workflows, this session offers practical lessons and hard-earned insights from the field.

items.title: Kargo in Action
items.summary:
Meet the Akuity engineers who built Kargo and wrote this book, Ken Cochrane, Jesse Suen, and Kent Rancourt. 

Kargo is a Kubernetes-native application lifecycle orchestration tool that works alongside Argo CD to promote software builds, automatically moving software artifacts, container images, Helm chart versions, or Git commits from development to staging to production.

In this session, we’ll ask these questions:
1. Why isn’t traditional CI/CD enough for modern software delivery?
2. Why should teams separate deployment from promotion?
3. How does Kargo close the gap between building software and running it safely?
4. How can teams promote the same artifact across multiple environments?
5. How does Kargo prevent configuration drift between environments?
6. What is a promotion control plane, and why do teams need one?
7. How can teams add approvals without slowing every release?
8. How does Kargo make software promotions auditable?
9. How can teams trace exactly what reached each environment?
10. How does Kargo make rollbacks safer and more predictable?
11. How can teams coordinate promotions across multiple services?
12. How does Kargo work with existing GitOps tools like Argo CD?
13. How can teams customize promotion workflows without creating fragile scripts?
14. How does Kargo help organizations balance delivery speed with governance?
15. What does a production-ready Kargo workflow look like end to end?

This is a live, interactive session, feel free to add your questions in the comments.
 
We will also giveaway Ebooks to 2 lucky winners during the session. Comment #KARGO to enter the raffle!

items.title: Start With One Word. Then Draw It.
items.summary: In episode 1019 of the SuperDataScience Podcast, @JonKrohnLearns talks with Priyanka Vergadia, better known to her quarter million strong developer community as the cloud girl, about her unique approach to finding familiar entry points when explaining technical concepts. She details a process that starts with identifying a single word for the concept, then finding a real-life visual representation, and finally mapping that to the technical explanation, emphasizing honesty when an analogy breaks down. This method helps make complex ideas accessible and memorable for diverse audiences.

items.title: Why IBM quantum computers are colder than space
items.summary:
IBM’s superconducting quantum computers don’t just require advanced quantum processors, they also rely on highly specialized systems to keep those processors operating in an environment that is stable, protected, and colder than the furthest reaches of outer space. As quantum computers scale, the infrastructure that houses, cools, and operates them must advance as well—delivering systems that are easier to maintain, upgrade, and link with other systems.  

In this episode of The Coherence Times, we’re joined by IBM’s Matt Hollister and Allie Lindler to dive deeper into the advanced cooling technology that makes superconducting quantum computing possible. Together, they discuss why cryogenic hardware matters, what goes into engineering refrigeration systems for the for modular quantum systems of the future, and how a new modular platform could help support the next generation quantum processors and systems.

items.title: Unveiling IBM's cryogenic modules to scale fault-tolerant quantum computing
items.summary:
IBM has successfully linked and cooled down the first operational modules of a scalable cryogenic system designed to support its fault-tolerant quantum computing mission. Connected together at an IBM Quantum facility in New York, the quantum fridges form IBM's first realization of the modular, shared, and ultra-cold environment required to operate multiple quantum processors. This milestone advances IBM's path to building IBM Quantum Starling, which is expected to be the world's first fault-tolerant quantum computer.

Learn more at: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog

items.title: Processing Large Financial Table with Sparrow Table Only Extraction
items.summary:
In this video I test Sparrow table only extraction mode on a large financial statement table. I use a 6 month property management sample data, with 51 rows and 7 columns, including section headers, blank spacer rows and multiple levels of subtotals.

Table only mode uses dots.ocr for table structure detection, combined with Sparrow custom processing logic on top, to produce a JSON array, with column headers mapped as keys. Section headers like INCOME and OPERATING EXPENSES are extracted too, with empty values, this way row order and table structure stay intact.

I go through the extraction result and compare it against the source table.
